Purpose

This note explains how risk acts throughout the main IT, governance, architecture, delivery, service, and cyber frameworks. It is designed as a reusable reference for a knowledge base and can support governance design, PMO/ITSM integration, architecture reviews, audit mapping, and executive communication.

The core idea is simple:

Risk is the thread that connects strategy, architecture, delivery, operations, security, resilience, assurance, and improvement.

Different frameworks emphasise different parts of the same risk chain.

Executive Summary

Across the main frameworks, risk tends to move through a common cycle:

Govern -> Design -> Deliver -> Operate -> Assure -> Improve

  • Govern sets appetite, tolerance, direction, and accountability.
  • Design turns risk into architecture principles, standards, controls, and investment choices.
  • Deliver manages uncertainty through projects, programmes, change, and supplier coordination.
  • Operate keeps live services, resilience, continuity, and security within acceptable limits.
  • Assure monitors, tests, audits, and reports.
  • Improve feeds lessons back into governance, architecture, and operations.

The frameworks differ mainly by where they place emphasis:

  • ISO 31000 provides the enterprise-wide risk logic.
  • COBIT governs and manages enterprise information and technology risk.
  • TOGAF reduces risk through better architecture and transition design.
  • PRINCE2 controls project-level uncertainty.
  • MSP controls programme and transformation risk.
  • ITIL manages service and operational risk.
  • NIST RMF / CSF formalise cyber and control-based risk management.
  • DORA turns ICT risk and resilience into regulatory obligations in financial services.

The Common Risk Pattern Across Frameworks

The end-to-end view

What happens in each stage

Stage What risk is doing Typical questions
Govern Defining direction and oversight What level of risk will we accept? Who owns what? What must be escalated?
Design Shaping architecture, policy, and controls How should we design this to reduce exposure? What standards or safeguards are needed?
Deliver Managing uncertainty in change What could stop delivery, delay value, or undermine outcomes?
Operate Controlling live operational risk Are services stable, secure, resilient, and supportable?
Assure Testing and verifying Are controls working? Are metrics and reports credible?
Improve Learning and adapting What should change in policy, design, controls, or delivery?

How Each Framework Treats Risk

ISO 31000

ISO 31000 is the umbrella discipline. It is not limited to IT. It provides a common language and structure for risk management across the enterprise. It is most useful when an organisation wants one coherent approach to risk across governance, projects, operations, architecture, security, and compliance.

Risk role in ISO 31000

  • Integrates risk into governance and decision-making
  • Provides principles and a management framework
  • Encourages consistent identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring, and communication
  • Supports a shared taxonomy and scoring model across disciplines

COBIT

COBIT treats risk as a matter of governance first, management second. It is strong where the organisation needs a structured connection between board oversight, executive accountability, control design, and assurance.

Risk role in COBIT

  • Board and executive focus on risk optimisation
  • Management translates risk direction into practices and controls
  • Risk is linked to security, continuity, suppliers, change, information, and assurance
  • Useful for integrating CIO, CISO, PMO, audit, and architecture views

Practical interpretation

COBIT is especially effective when you want to answer questions such as:

  • Are we governing IT risk properly?
  • Are accountabilities clear?
  • Are we balancing value, risk, and resources?
  • Is our assurance model coherent?

ITIL

ITIL treats risk as part of value delivery through services. It does not approach risk mainly as board theory; it approaches it as a practical concern in operating and improving digital services.

Risk role in ITIL

  • Embedded in service design, transition, support, and improvement
  • Present in incident, problem, change enablement, supplier, security, monitoring, and continuity practices
  • Focuses on service stability, quality, resilience, and operational visibility

Practical interpretation

ITIL is most useful when the question is:

  • How do we keep risk under control while running live services?
  • How do we reduce service disruption and change failure?
  • How do we improve resilience, supportability, and customer value?

TOGAF

TOGAF acts on risk before delivery starts in earnest by improving structure. It reduces risk through architecture principles, standards, target-state thinking, transition architecture, and roadmap choices.

Risk role in TOGAF

  • Reduces structural risk through better design
  • Addresses complexity, integration, obsolescence, standards, and technology alignment
  • Strengthens security and resilience by embedding them into architecture decisions

Practical interpretation

TOGAF helps answer:

  • Are we designing avoidable risk into the estate?
  • Are our standards increasing or reducing exposure?
  • Are transition plans realistic and controlled?

PRINCE2

PRINCE2 handles risk in a controlled project environment. It is concerned with uncertainty that could affect scope, cost, schedule, quality, and continued business justification.

Risk role in PRINCE2

  • Identifies and assesses project-level risks
  • Defines owners, actions, responses, and escalation paths
  • Uses stage control and exception-based management
  • Links risk to decision points and business case viability

Practical interpretation

PRINCE2 is useful when the question is:

  • Will this project still deliver what it promised?
  • What threatens schedule, scope, cost, or quality?
  • When should the issue be escalated or re-planned?

MSP

MSP treats risk at transformation scale rather than single-project scale. It is concerned with whether a programme will land successfully, coordinate its dependencies, achieve desired outcomes, and realise benefits.

Risk role in MSP

  • Manages uncertainty across multiple projects and workstreams
  • Focuses on dependency risk, benefit risk, organisational change risk, stakeholder risk, and governance risk
  • Supports tranche-based decisions and transformation control

Practical interpretation

MSP is valuable when the question becomes:

  • Will the programme achieve strategic outcomes, not just outputs?
  • Are the interdependencies being managed effectively?
  • Is change adoption or benefits realisation at risk?

NIST RMF

NIST RMF formalises risk in a structured security and privacy life cycle. It is control-oriented and evidence-driven.

Risk role in NIST RMF

  • Categorises information systems and data sensitivity
  • Selects and tailors controls
  • Implements and assesses those controls
  • Supports authorisation decisions and ongoing monitoring

Practical interpretation

NIST RMF is strong when the organisation asks:

  • What controls are required for this system?
  • Are those controls operating effectively?
  • Can this system be authorised or remain in service?

NIST CSF

NIST CSF provides an outcome-based cybersecurity structure. It is particularly helpful for executive communication because it links governance to operational cyber capabilities.

Risk role in NIST CSF

  • Frames cyber risk through Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
  • Supports target-state design and maturity improvement
  • Connects cyber operations with leadership communication and prioritisation

DORA

DORA makes ICT risk and operational resilience a matter of regulatory discipline in the financial sector.

Risk role in DORA

  • Requires structured ICT risk management
  • Emphasises digital operational resilience
  • Requires incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party oversight
  • Pushes resilience from good practice into formal compliance obligations

How Risk Flows Across the Layers of an IT Operating Model

Layer interpretation

Operating layer Risk emphasis Best-fit frameworks
Board / Executive / CIO Appetite, tolerance, oversight, accountability ISO 31000, COBIT, NIST CSF, DORA
Enterprise architecture Structural, standards, integration, technology, resilience risk TOGAF, COBIT
Portfolio / Programme / Project Investment, transformation, delivery, dependency, benefits risk MSP, PRINCE2, COBIT
Service operations Stability, support, continuity, supplier, change, operational risk ITIL, COBIT
Cybersecurity / privacy Threat, vulnerability, control, resilience, recovery risk NIST RMF, NIST CSF, ISO 27001-style overlays
Audit / assurance Evidence, testing, reporting, challenge, monitoring COBIT, NIST, internal audit methods

One Enterprise Risk Language, Multiple Framework Views

A common organisational mistake is to let each framework create its own separate risk universe.

That often leads to:

  • separate risk registers
  • conflicting scoring methods
  • duplicated controls
  • inconsistent escalation paths
  • fragmented reporting to executives
  • poor traceability from policy to operation

A better model is:

Unified approach

  • One enterprise risk taxonomy
  • One scoring model
  • One escalation model
  • One reporting logic
  • Many framework-specific views

In that model:

  • COBIT provides the governance and assurance view
  • TOGAF provides the design and architecture view
  • PRINCE2 / MSP provide the delivery and transformation view
  • ITIL provides the live service view
  • NIST provides the cyber-control view
  • DORA provides the regulatory resilience overlay where relevant

Audit, assure, and improve Strong Strong Moderate Moderate Moderate Strong Strong Strong

Example: One Risk Seen Through Multiple Frameworks

Example risk

Critical cloud provider outage affecting a customer-facing platform

How each framework would see it

Framework Interpretation of the same risk
ISO 31000 Enterprise risk requiring assessment, treatment, monitoring, ownership, and communication
COBIT Governance issue involving supplier oversight, resilience, continuity, security, and executive accountability
TOGAF Architecture concern requiring redundancy, failover, recovery design, and standards review
PRINCE2 Project or transition dependency risk if implementation relies on the provider
MSP Programme dependency and business outcome risk if multiple projects rely on the same platform
ITIL Operational continuity, incident, problem, supplier, and change concern for live services
NIST RMF / CSF Security and resilience control issue requiring safeguards, monitoring, response, and recovery
DORA ICT third-party and operational resilience issue with compliance and reporting implications in finance

Recommended Integrated Model

For an enterprise IT governance model, a practical combination is:

Recommended backbone

  • ISO 31000 as the common risk method and language
  • COBIT for governance, accountability, assurance, and control alignment
  • TOGAF for design-time risk reduction
  • MSP / PRINCE2 for transformation and delivery control
  • ITIL for operational risk and service resilience
  • NIST CSF / RMF for cyber and control depth
  • DORA / NIS2 / ISO 27001 as regulatory and control overlays where relevant

End-to-end operating logic

Key Takeaways

  1. Risk is not separate from IT frameworks; it is one of their main connecting threads.
  2. Each framework sees a different part of the same risk system.
  3. COBIT is strongest for governance, accountability, and assurance.
  4. TOGAF reduces risk through design.
  5. PRINCE2 and MSP reduce risk through controlled change.
  6. ITIL reduces risk in live services.
  7. NIST deepens cyber and control rigour.
  8. DORA makes resilience and ICT risk formal obligations in regulated finance.
  9. The best enterprise model uses one risk language with multiple framework views.
